title: The monkey and the kitten
hookLine: a baby monkey clings to its mother, a kitten is carried in its mother's mouth, and Ramanuja's followers asked which one you are
carry: prapatti: taking refuge in God's grace
tomorrow: You are that, or you are his?

lines: HOW MUCH DOES THE SOUL HOLD ON?
cards: A mother monkey leaps from branch to branch. Her baby rides along, holding on to her belly with its own small hands. A mother cat moves her kitten another way.
She picks it up by the scruff of its neck, and the kitten just hangs there, loose, carried. Two babies, two mothers, two ways of getting across.
In South India, Ramanuja's later followers argued over these two animals, because the question underneath them is a big one. When God saves a soul, how much does the soul hold on?

teach.h: YOU CAN'T BE CARRIED BY YOURSELF.
teach.b: You met Ramanuja a few days ago, on the temple tower, with the world as God's body. Today, the heart of how his followers practice: prapatti, surrender, taking refuge. Not giving up.
Turning to God the way a child turns to a parent, and letting yourself be held.
Sri Vaishnavas say Ramanuja himself, at the temple of Srirangam, offered a prose prayer of surrender before Vishnu and Lakshmi, and they still recite it.
They treasure a verse near the end of the Gita, which they call the final verse.

teach.h: TAKE REFUGE IN ME ALONE. DO NOT GRIEVE.
teach.b: Krishna says, roughly: let go of every other support, take refuge in me alone, I will free you from every wrong, do not grieve. Later came the question from the hook.

teach.h: THE MONKEY HOLDS ON. THE KITTEN IS CARRIED.
teach.b: One lineage, later called the northern school, taught with the baby monkey: grace carries you, and you also hold on, with your own small effort.
The other, the southern school, taught with the kitten: grace does everything, and even your holding on is a gift.
Both lineages trace themselves to Ramanuja, and both are alive today. This path doesn't settle it. But both pictures share something: a mother and a child.
Two. Surrender only makes sense if there's someone to surrender to.

teach.h: PRAPATTI: TAKING REFUGE IN GOD'S GRACE.
teach.b: Advaita would say that in the end there's only one. Ramanuja's people say the soul is held, forever, and never stops being the one who is held. That's devotion needing difference.
You can't be carried by yourself.

how: Many Sri Vaishnavas formally take refuge through a rite called samashrayana, given by a teacher, and recite the dvaya mantra and Gita 18.66 daily; the northern (Vadakalai) and southern (Tenkalai) lineages are often told apart by the shape of the namam, the mark worn on the forehead.

o: giving up on effort and simply doing nothing
taking refuge in God, letting yourself be held
a strict vow of fasting and silence at a temple

s: for Ramanuja's followers, surrender means the soul disappears into God
the soul stays itself forever; surrender is a relationship, a child held by a parent.
Ramanuja's later followers disagreed about how much the soul holds on
one lineage pictured a baby monkey clinging, the other a kitten carried; both trace themselves to Ramanuja.
prapatti means giving up and doing nothing
it means taking refuge: turning to God and letting yourself be held.

games.q: two lineages of Ramanuja's followers disagree: is the soul a baby monkey that clings, or a kitten that's carried? what did the tradition do?
o: keep the monkey and drop the kitten.
keep both: two lineages, each tracing itself to Ramanuja.
keep the kitten and drop the monkey.
games.why: both lineages are alive today. and in both pictures there's a mother and a child: two, and the space between is love.

practice: Feel the chair or the floor under you: you aren't holding yourself up right now, something else is.
Notice one small effort you're still making, a tight jaw, a held breath, and let it go; you don't have to decide whether you're the monkey or the kitten, just notice what it feels like to be held.
If you pray, name one worry and leave it with God for these few minutes.

wordCard.voice: Prapatti, taking refuge, the way of Ramanuja's followers. Clinging like a monkey or carried like a kitten, there is always a mother and a child. Two.

orig.note: Sanskrit: surrender, taking refuge; from pra + pad, to go forward toward, to approach for shelter.

carryVoice: Your line: prapatti, taking refuge in God's grace. Held, and still yourself. Two ninety-two, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.66 (the charama shloka: take refuge in me alone; do not grieve)
Sharanagati Gadya, traditionally attributed to Ramanuja (the prayer of surrender at Srirangam)
Later Sri Vaishnava teaching: the monkey and cat analogies of the Vadakalai and Tenkalai lineages (Vedanta Desika; Pillai Lokacharya)
